title: Atrahasis
subtitle: the Babylonian story of how the gods made humankind and sent the Flood
lead: Atrahasis is a Babylonian poem about the age before the Flood. It begins when the gods themselves had to do all the work of the world. The lesser gods dig the rivers until they rebel, so the wise god Enki has a god slain and the birth goddess Mami mixes his flesh and blood with clay to make humankind, who will carry the gods' work basket instead. Then people multiply, and their noise keeps the chief god Enlil awake. He sends plague, drought and famine, and at last a flood. Enki warns one man, Atrahasis, whose name means "exceedingly wise", to build a boat. After seven days and seven nights the gods, starved of offerings, gather over his sacrifice, and they set new limits on human life. (The broken line is restored "like flies", the picture the Epic of Gilgamesh uses for the same scene.)

It is not Scripture for anyone. It is the sacred story of the gods of ancient Babylon, and no church or synagogue has ever read it as the word of God. It is on this site for three reasons Matt chose: it gives the world of Genesis 1–11 more context, it is a great and moving piece of ancient writing, and it shows how another people told the same story Genesis tells, the making of humankind and the Flood, and where the two stories part. The translation is made fresh from the Akkadian, the language of Babylon. The notes describe the poem fairly and then measure it, as a Christian reader would, by the Bible.
facts: The gods and temples of ancient Babylonia and Assyria, whose scribes copied it for more than a thousand years. No living church or synagogue reads it as scripture.
Its first words, inūma ilū awīlum, "When the gods were man" (the meaning is debated: see 1:1)
Unknown. The best copy was made by a junior scribe, Ipiq-Aya, at Sippar in Babylonia.

The best copy: the 11th and 12th years of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (SEAL dates Tablet II's year to about 1628 BC; Millard rounds it to about 1630 BC). The poem itself is older; how much older is unknown.
Old Babylonian Akkadian, a Semitic language (a cousin of Hebrew) written in cuneiform on clay tablets
Old Babylonian copies from Sippar and Larsa; later copies from Babylon, Nippur, Ugarit and Hattusa, from the Assyrian royal library at Nineveh, and from late Babylonian Sippar
A narrative poem (epic or myth) in pairs of echoing lines, with long speeches and repeated passages
Three tablets, 1,245 lines by the ancient scribe's count; on this site 12 chapters and 1,232 verses (one verse per tablet line, with each run of lost lines as one verse)
authorship: No ancient copy names an author. The colophons (the notes a scribe wrote at the end of a tablet) say who copied it: Ipiq-Aya, the "junior scribe", on each of the three tablets of the Sippar copy, with the day and the royal year (SEAL's English for the same title on Tablet II is "apprentice scribe"). The scribe wrote "new break" where the tablet he was copying was damaged, so even this oldest dated copy was copied from an older one (Heidel; Clay). The scribe's name is read Ipiq-Aya by SEAL, following Wilcke; Clay, who edited the second tablet in 1922, read it Azag-Aya (SEAL also lists an earlier publication of that tablet, by Scheil in 1898).

The poem was composed in Babylonia, in Akkadian, some time before about 1630 BC. Millard wrote in 1967 that how much earlier it was composed "cannot yet be said", and that is still the honest answer. Heidel placed the first written Babylonian flood stories at the end of the third millennium or the start of the second (about 2000 BC). Older Sumerian traditions lie behind it: the Sumerian Flood Story tells of a flood hero called Ziusudra (Heidel). Later scribes reworked it: the Middle Babylonian and Assyrian copies often differ from the Old Babylonian one in wording and sometimes in order, and the flood part was reused in Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the hero is called Utnapishtim and also "Atrahasis" (Heidel; Millard).
A minority view: a western origin

Albert Clay (1922) argued that the story was not Babylonian at root but "a very ancient Hebrew or Amorite Deluge Story", brought into Babylonia by western Semites, and that Israel's traditions were native to the land of the Amorites rather than borrowed from Babylon. He based this on words in the Old Babylonian copy that he took to be western, above all ḫubūru. SEAL's glossary takes ḫubūru as an ordinary Akkadian word ("bustle, clamour"; the Plain says "uproar"), and the editions used here read the poem as Babylonian Akkadian. The sources opened for this page name no later scholar who holds Clay's view; it belongs to the history of the question.

Christian scholars who believe Genesis add a further question: where did the memory itself come from? Alan Millard (1967) wrote that if the Flood took place, knowledge of it must have survived to form the accounts we have, and that the Babylonians could only describe it in the language of their many gods, while the Hebrews, or their ancestors, understood it as the act of God. On that view the poem's authors were Babylonian scribes, but the event they were remembering was real.

audience.to: Its first users that we can name were scribes. The best copy was written by Ipiq-Aya, a "junior scribe", at Sippar, a city on the Euphrates north of Babylon, in the 11th and 12th years of King Ammi-saduqa (the 1600s BC). He counted the lines of each tablet (416, 439 and 390, "total 1,245 for 3 tablets") and dated each one by the king's year names, which recall statues of the king and the building of Dur-Ammi-saduqa at the mouth of the Euphrates. Later the poem was copied far and wide: at Larsa, Babylon and Nippur, at Ugarit on the Syrian coast and at Hattusa in Anatolia, in the Assyrian royal library at Nineveh, and again at Sippar in late Babylonian times. The poem also speaks to listeners: its last lines call it a song for the gods to hear in praise of a god, and the singer tells all the people that he has sung of the flood and calls them to listen (12:102–103).
audience.why: It answered the deepest questions its hearers had, in the terms of their religion. Why do people exist? To carry the gods' work so the gods can rest. Why must we work, and feed the gods with offerings? Because that is what we were made for, and the Flood showed the gods how hungry they are without us. Why do people die, why are some women barren, why do babies die, and why may some priestesses not bear children? Because after the Flood the gods set limits on human numbers. And it taught them to honor their gods: when the plague came, the people turned their offerings to the plague god Namtar and he lifted his hand (chapter 5). Knowing this changes how it reads beside Genesis. Genesis was written for Israel, a people who had to live among nations that told stories like this one, and it answers the same questions very differently: humankind made in God's image and blessed, God resting without needing anyone to feed him, a flood sent for violence rather than noise, and a covenant afterward that says "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1).
views: The colophons name the copyist and his rank, count the lines and date each tablet: the Sippar copy is the careful work of a junior scribe. Copies from Ugarit and Hattusa show that the story, or something of it, was known far outside Babylonia by about 1300 BC (Millard).
A song in praise of a god
The poem ends by calling itself a song for the Igigi gods to hear in praise of a god addressed as counselor of the gods (12:98–103). It was meant to be performed, not only copied.
Clay (1922) held that the late Assyrian version had been put into a magical setting for incantations.

outline: When the gods did the work: the great gods cast lots for sky, earth and the Apsu, and the lesser gods dig the rivers (Tablet I 1–38)
The gods' strike: they burn their tools, surround Enlil's house at night, and Nusku, Anu and Enlil debate what to do (I 39–173)
Enki's plan: a god is slain, and the birth goddess Mami mixes his flesh and blood with clay to make humankind to carry the gods' work basket (I 174–260)
The birth goddesses shape seven men and seven women; the customs of birth and marriage; a broken stretch (I 261–351)
Humankind multiplies, its noise keeps Enlil awake, and he sends plague; Enki tells Atrahasis how to end it through Namtar (I 352–416)
Another 1,200 years; the noise again, and Enlil holds back the rain (Tablet II, segments A–D)
The rain withheld again, the sky and the deep locked shut, and the famine years (II E 1–78y)
Atrahasis pleads with his god; Enki's answer; the worst years of famine; the end of the second tablet's story of hunger (II E 79–175, F)
Enki lets the fish loose; the gods meet in council; they swear an oath to send the flood, and Enki refuses to join it (II G–I)
The dream and the reed wall: build a boat; the excuse to the elders; loading the boat; the feast; the door sealed (III i–ii)
The flood for seven days and seven nights; the gods afraid, hungry and thirsty; Nintu's lament for her children (III iii–iv)
The offering and the flies; Enlil's anger; Enki's answer; the new order of death, barren women and priestesses; the closing song and the scribe's colophon (III v–viii)

lenses.name: Christian reading
lenses.desc: How a Christian who believes the Genesis account reads the poem: what it shares with the Bible, what it bends or leaves out, and what the Bible says instead. This is the site's own voice.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Assyriologists and biblical scholars: the dates and copies, what the poem meant in Babylon, and the theories of how Genesis relates to it (borrowing, a common source, deliberate reply), each with the scholars who hold it.

lenses.name: Mesopotamian religion
lenses.desc: What the first hearers believed: the gods and their ranks, temples and offerings, omens, birth customs, and the scribal schools that copied the poem.

lenses.name: Spiritual reading
lenses.desc: Christian readings of the unseen world: the gods of the nations as nothing, as demons, or as fallen members of God's heavenly council; the rebel gods and the Watchers. Always labeled as readings, with the people who hold them.

lenses.name: Jewish and early Christian writings
lenses.desc: Where 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Genesis Apocryphon, the Book of Giants, Josephus, Berossus (as later writers quote him), the church fathers and the rabbis tell the same events or use the same pictures.

sections.b:
Read it first as its hearers did: as a story told by people who believed in many gods and were asking real questions. Why do we work so hard? Why do we die? Why did the Flood come? Then read it beside Genesis 1–11, which tells the same span of time, from the making of humankind to the Flood and the new start after it. The notes mark where the two agree, where they differ, and where Genesis seems to answer back.

Watch for three things. Work: the poem begins with gods who hate their work, and humankind is made to take it over (chapters 1–3). Noise: humankind multiplies and its noise keeps Enlil awake, and every disaster after that is meant to silence it (chapters 5–9). Food: when the Flood wipes out the people, the gods go hungry and thirsty, and they gather over the first sacrifice (chapters 11–12). Genesis has its own words for each of these: work given as a gift (Genesis 2:15), evil and violence rather than noise (Genesis 6:5, 11), and a God who smells the offering but does not need it (Genesis 8:21).

The poem is broken in many places. Where the clay is lost, the text says so, and the notes say only what the surviving lines support.

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Akkadian text of the score editions of Sources of Early Akkadian Literature (SEAL), edited by M. P. Streck and N. Wasserman, which print every surviving copy line by line. Each verse is one line of the clay tablet: Tablet I is numbered by line (I 1 to I 416), Tablet II by the segments SEAL arranges in story order (II A to II I), and Tablet III by its eight columns. The twelve chapters are cut at the episodes of the story. Words that SEAL restores from another copy or a repeated passage are translated as text; where nothing can be restored, the Plain shows "...", and a run of lost lines is one verse in parentheses saying how much is missing.

Akkadian poetry comes in pairs of lines that say a thing twice in different words. The Plain keeps each line on its own verse so the pairs show. Repeated passages (the speech formulas, the strike speech, the cycles of plague, drought and famine) are rendered the same way each time, as the poem repeats them. The gods are written with a small "god"; "God" and "the LORD" are used on this site only for the God of the Bible. The boat is "the boat", never "the ark", which is the site's word for Noah's vessel.

Where the copies differ in a way that changes the meaning, the variants name each copy by SEAL's letter (its siglum) and say which one the Plain follows.

SEAL lists the manuscripts of each tablet by letter (its siglum), museum number, place and period:

  • Old Babylonian (the 1600s BC and earlier): the three-tablet copy of Ipiq-Aya from Sippar (Tablet I is ms. A, British Museum BM 78941+78943; Tablet II is ms. B, MLC 1889, the tablet Clay published in 1922; Tablet III is ms. C, BM 78942+ with a joining piece, MAH 16064), other Old Babylonian pieces of Tablets I and II, and a copy of the flood section from Larsa (the Schøyen tablet, MS 5108).
  • Middle Babylonian: pieces from Babylon, from Nippur (CBS 13532, in Philadelphia), from Ugarit (RS 22.421, in Damascus) and from Hattusa, the Hittite capital (KBo 36, 26); Millard dates the Ugarit and Hattusa pieces about 1300 BC. SEAL also files the Ark Tablet with these copies: a tablet of unknown origin in which the god speaks to the reed wall and the hero then tells how he built a round boat and brought the wild animals in "two by two".
  • Neo-Assyrian (the 600s BC): many fragments from the royal library at Nineveh (museum numbers beginning K., Sm. and Bu.), which sometimes order or word the story differently.
  • Late Babylonian: copies from Sippar, now in Baghdad (IM 124646 and 124649, and IM 132665, a tablet that quotes a few lines), and a piece probably from Babylon.

No copy is complete. Together they preserve most of Tablet I, a large part of Tablet II, and the flood story of Tablet III, with large gaps in each. Tablet II rests largely on one Old Babylonian copy (B), and Tablet III on one (C).

The poem has a ranked family of gods. Anu is the father and king, in the sky. Enlil is the warrior and counselor who rules the earth; he sends every disaster. Enki (called Ea in the later copies) lives in the Apsu, the fresh waters under the earth; he is the clever god who devises humankind and saves Atrahasis, his "servant". Mami, also called Nintu and Belet-ili, is the birth goddess who shapes people. The Anunnaki are the great gods; the Igigi are the gods who did the work and went on strike. Smaller figures include Nusku, Enlil's minister; Ninurta and Ennugi; Namtar, the god of plague; Adad, the storm god; and Nisaba, the goddess of grain.

This is not the world of the Bible, where there is one God who made everything and needs nothing (Isaiah 44:9; Acts 17:24–25). The notes explain what the first hearers believed about each god, and how Christians have understood such gods (see "How a Christian reads it").

sections.h: Atrahasis and Genesis 1–11, side by side
sections.b:
Atrahasis is the one Babylonian work that runs, like Genesis 1–9, from the making of humankind to the Flood and the order of life after it (Millard). The outline is shared; nearly everything else differs:

  • Why humans exist: to carry the gods' basket (3:17–22), or to bear God's image and rule and tend his world (Genesis 1:26–28; Genesis 2:15).
  • What humans are made of: clay with the flesh and blood of a slain god (3:48–58), or dust of the ground and the breath of God (Genesis 2:7).
  • Why the Flood came: the noise of humankind kept Enlil awake (5:1–10), or "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:11).
  • Who decides: gods who quarrel, swear oaths and blame each other (9:15; 12:30–40), or one God who is grieved, judges and saves (Genesis 6:6–8).
  • After the Flood: barren women, a demon who snatches babies, and priestesses who must not bear (12:68–76), or "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1) and a covenant with every living thing (Genesis 9:8–17).

For the same comparison from the Genesis side, see the note at Genesis 2:7 on the man made from the ground, the box on humans made from clay on the Genesis 2 page, the box on the flood in Atrahasis on the Genesis 7 page, the note at Genesis 8:21 on the gods gathering over the sacrifice, and the topic page on the ancient Near East.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a world that needed relief from its basket
spec.body: In Atrahasis, work is the reason humankind exists: the gods hated their basket and made people to carry it (3:17–22). Genesis also knows that work became hard (Genesis 3:17–19), but it says the opposite about why: work was given before the fall as care for God's garden (Genesis 2:15), and when Lamech names his son he hopes for an end to the curse: "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful labor of our hands, from the ground that the LORD cursed" (Genesis 5:29). In a world whose most famous story said that humans were made to carry the gods' load, the name Noah, "rest", would sound like an answer. Jesus speaks to the same weariness: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). This is my own reading; I have not found it argued in what I read for this page, though Millard and Hasel both stress the contrast in why humans were made.

spec.title: Claude's theory: three oaths about the Flood
spec.body: Atrahasis turns on an oath: the gods "swore an oath together" to wipe out humankind (9:15; 12:33), and Enki will not break it openly, so he speaks to a wall. In 1 Enoch the rebel Watchers also bind themselves by an oath together before they come down to earth (1 Enoch 6:4–5), and the Flood follows their crime. The Bible's oath runs the other way: after the Flood God swears never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:11; Isaiah 54:9). If the three stories remember one event, the Babylonian oath is an oath to destroy, the Enochic oath is an oath to sin, and God's oath is an oath to spare. This pattern is my own observation, offered as a way to read the stories side by side, not as proof that one borrowed from another.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the flies at the necklace and the bow in the clouds
spec.body: After the Flood, Mami takes the "flies" of lapis lazuli that Anu hung up and says they will be around her neck so that she will remember those days (12:20–29). In Genesis God sets his bow in the clouds: "my bow I have put in the clouds, and it will be the sign of a covenant between me and the earth" (Genesis 9:13), and when he sees it, "then I will remember my covenant" (Genesis 9:15). Both stories end the Flood with a sign hung up in view of a divine person, so that he or she will remember. The difference is the heart of the matter: the goddess remembers her grief over a disaster her own council caused; God remembers a promise he made to every living thing. The broken lines (12:26–29) make any comparison uncertain, so I offer this as a possibility only.

traditions.q: How do Catholic, evangelical and Adventist statements on Genesis 1–11 as history bear on its likeness to Mesopotamian stories such as Atrahasis?
views: Pius XII taught that the first eleven chapters of Genesis belong to history in a true sense, told in simple, figurative language suited to their first readers. If the sacred writers took anything from the popular stories of their people, God's inspiration guided them in choosing and judging it, and such stories are not to be put on the same level as myths (Humani generis 38–39). The Catechism says of the fall that Genesis 3 "uses figurative language, but affirms a primeval event" (Catechism 390). Neither text names the Mesopotamian stories, but Humani generis allows that Genesis may draw on older popular stories without becoming myth.

The Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (1982) affirms that Genesis 1–11 is factual, as is the rest of the book, and denies that its teachings are mythical (Article XXII). It does not mention the Mesopotamian stories, but on its view the likenesses cannot come from Genesis turning myths into Scripture. Alan Millard's conclusion fits that view: Atrahasis and Genesis "undoubtedly describe the same Flood", and borrowing by the Hebrews has not been shown.

The church's Fundamental Belief 6 says that God "has revealed in Scripture the authentic and historical account of His creative activity", in a recent six-day creation, and that the first man and woman were made in God's image "as the crowning work of Creation". It does not address the Mesopotamian stories. Gerhard Hasel, writing from Andrews University, a Seventh-day Adventist university, argued that Genesis 1 is not dependent on the Babylonian stories but deliberately written against them: where Atrahasis makes humankind to relieve the gods of their labor, Genesis 1 makes humankind the "pinnacle of creation".

canon.summary: Atrahasis is a sacred poem of ancient Babylon, about its gods, the making of humankind and the Flood. No church or synagogue has ever counted it as Scripture. It is translated here for context and comparison, and read from a Christian standpoint that takes the Bible as true.
accepted_by: Babylonian and Assyrian scribes and temples (about 1700–500 BC)

Held in honor, not as a fixed scripture in our sense, but as a poem about the gods that scribes copied, studied and performed for more than a thousand years. The poem calls itself a song for the gods to hear in praise of a god (12:98–103). Its copies come from the hands of scribes (the Sippar copy's "junior scribe"), from the Assyrian royal library at Nineveh, and from Sippar again in late Babylonian times.

Never Scripture. Israel's Scripture tells the Flood through Noah (Genesis 6–9). The Jewish historian Josephus knew the Babylonian flood story through Berossus, a Babylonian priest who wrote in Greek. He quoted him, with Hieronymus the Egyptian and Nicolaus of Damascus, as outside witnesses that the ark had come to rest in Armenia ("all the writers of barbarian histories make mention of this flood", Jewish Antiquities 1.93–95, numbered 1.3.6 in Whiston's translation): writers of the nations who agreed with Moses, not authorities beside him.

Never Scripture in any church, Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant or other. The Bible says the gods of the nations are "a nothing-god" (Psalm 96:5) and warns against worshiping them. Christians read the poem, as they read other ancient texts, for background to Genesis, and Christian scholars have studied it closely since its discovery (Heidel; Millard).
No living religious community reads it as scripture. It is studied by Assyriologists and biblical scholars and read as one of the great works of the ancient world.

provenance.b: The best copy was made at Sippar in Babylonia by the junior scribe Ipiq-Aya, on three large tablets. Each tablet ends with a colophon. Tablet I: "Tablet 1 of inūma ilū awīlum", 416 lines, written on the 21st of the month Nisan, in a year named for two statues of the king, which SEAL identifies as his 12th year. Tablet II: 439 lines, the 28th of Shabatu, in the year Ammi-saduqa built Dur-Ammi-saduqa at the mouth of the Euphrates, which SEAL identifies as his 11th year, about 1628 BC. Tablet III: 390 lines, "total 1,245 for 3 tablets", in the month Ayyaru of his 12th year (SEAL). Ammi-saduqa was the next-to-last king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (Heidel), the dynasty of Hammurabi. When Clay published the second tablet in 1922 he dated the same year to 1966 BC, by the chronology of his day; the dates now used are much later.

Ipiq-Aya marked places where his model was broken ("new break"), so he was copying an older tablet (Heidel; Clay). How old the poem is cannot be known from the copies. Sumerian flood traditions are older still: the Sumerian Flood Story has a hero, Ziusudra, warned by a god and saved in a huge boat (Heidel). Heidel judged that the first written Babylonian flood stories go back to the end of the third or the start of the second millennium BC (around 2000 BC).

The poem spread across the ancient Near East. Middle Babylonian copies come from Babylon and Nippur, and versions of the flood story were copied at Ugarit on the Syrian coast and at Hattusa in Anatolia, about 1300 BC (Millard). Assyrian scribes copied it for the royal library at Nineveh in the 600s BC, in a form that sometimes words or orders the story differently; Clay thought this late version had been put into a magical setting for use in incantations. Late Babylonian scribes at Sippar copied it again. Its flood section was reworked into Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the hero Utnapishtim is also called "Atrahasis". In the 200s BC Berossus, a priest of Marduk at Babylon, wrote a history in Greek (the Babyloniaca of Berossus) whose flood hero, Xisuthros, carries the name of Ziusudra; only excerpts survive, through later writers (Heidel).

The poem was forgotten when cuneiform stopped being read. Pieces were found in the 1800s and early 1900s among the tablets dug at Nineveh and Sippar, but most of the story was not known until the British Museum's Old Babylonian tablets were published in 1965. Millard said in his lecture of 1966 that until then about a fifth of the story had been known, and that four-fifths could now be restored. W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard published the standard edition in 1969. More pieces have been found since, among them the late copies from Sippar (published in 1996), the Schøyen tablet from Larsa and the Ark Tablet, and SEAL now prints all of them line by line.

rejected_why.h: It is the story of other gods
rejected_why.b: Atrahasis is a sacred story of Babylon's gods: Anu, Enlil, Enki, Mami and the rest. The first commandment forbids Israel to have other gods, and the prophets say that such gods are nothing: "Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god, but the LORD made the heavens" (Psalm 96:5). Paul says the same to the church: "an idol is nothing in the world," and "there is no God but one" (1 Corinthians 8:4). So neither Jews nor Christians could read a hymn to these gods as God's word.

rejected_why.h: Its gods are not the God of the prophets and apostles
rejected_why.b: The gods of the poem are tired, quarrelsome and hungry. They hate their work, they cannot sleep for noise, they decide on destruction without thinking it through, and they crowd around a sacrifice because they are starving. The God of the Bible "does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4), and "Nor do human hands tend to him, as if he were short of anything. It is he who gives life and breath and all things to everyone" (Acts 17:25).

rejected_why.h: Its Flood differs from Genesis at the root
rejected_why.b: In Atrahasis the Flood is sent because human noise disturbs a god's sleep, and it comes from a divided council. The hero is saved because his god breaks ranks. Afterward the gods curb human numbers. In Genesis, God sends the Flood because "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:11), saves Noah because he "found favor in the LORD's eyes" (Genesis 6:8), and afterward blesses humankind and makes a covenant with every living thing (Genesis 9:1, 8–17). Christians who read Genesis as the true account, as this site does, read this one as another people's telling of the same events in the language of their gods (Millard). The Jewish historian Josephus treated the nations' flood stories in a similar way, as witnesses that agreed with Moses (Jewish Antiquities 1.93–95).

rejected_why.h: No one ever claimed it as revelation from the God of Israel
rejected_why.b: Unlike 1 Enoch or Tobit, Atrahasis was never read in a synagogue or a church, never claimed by any Jewish or Christian group, and never debated as a candidate for the canon. Its place on this site is as a witness to another people's beliefs, translated so that readers can compare it with Scripture.

christian_view.h: What it remembers that the Bible also says
christian_view.b: Read beside Genesis, Atrahasis keeps a surprising amount of the same outline. Humankind was made, not born from the gods, and made from earth; both stories also give humans something from the divine side, though the two gifts are very different: a slain god's flesh and blood here, God's own breath in Genesis 2:7. Millard notes that both stress man's earthy part and his divine part equally. People were made to work (Genesis 2:15). Male and female were made together, and marriage belongs to the order of creation (chapter 4; Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24). People multiplied (Genesis 6:1). A flood destroyed them, but one man was warned, built a boat, brought his family and animals into it, and was shut in (Genesis 6:13–7:16). The storm is counted in sevens (11:74; Genesis 7:4, 10). Afterward he offered a sacrifice, and heaven took notice of it: the gods gathered over it, and the LORD smelled Noah's offering (12:8; Genesis 8:20–21). After the Flood came a new order for human life. A Christian who believes Genesis can read these likenesses as what Millard called the memory of the same Flood, kept by both peoples, and told by the Babylonians in the language of their gods.

christian_view.h: What it bends or leaves out
christian_view.b: Almost everything that gives the story its meaning is different. There is no one Creator; the world is already there, and the gods divide it by lot. Humankind is made as a slave class so that the gods can rest, not as the image of God and his blessed ruler over the earth (Genesis 1:26–28). The fault that brings the Flood is noise, not sin; Heidel noted that in Genesis the Flood is a righteous punishment for sin, while in the Babylonian stories the reason is far less plain: in the Epic of Gilgamesh it is "not nearly so apparent", and in Atrahasis it is the people's noise. The gods do not grieve over evil (Genesis 6:6) but over their own hunger. The hero is saved by a trick, a god speaking to a wall to get around an oath, not by grace (Genesis 6:8). And the story ends with barrenness, infant death and women who must not bear, where Genesis ends with a blessing to fill the earth and a covenant sign in the clouds (Genesis 9:1, 12–17). As Heidel put it, the skeleton is the same, but the flesh and blood and the spirit are different.

christian_view.h: Did Genesis borrow it? Every answer
christian_view.b:
The likenesses are real, and every serious reader has to explain them. The answers fall into five groups.

  • Genesis reworked Mesopotamian stories. L. W. King (1918) thought the Hebrews met Babylonian legends in Canaan, where Babylonian was the language of learning, and again under Assyrian rule. Millard reported in 1967 that most commentators then held that Israel adopted and adapted the Babylonian creation story, Enuma Elish, through Canaanite sources.
  • Both come from an older tradition. Gerhard von Rad held that Genesis and the Babylonian flood story are "independent arrangements of a still older tradition", perhaps Sumerian, which Israel met in Canaan and made its own; Millard quotes this as the widespread view of his day. Alexander Heidel (1949) found the case for Hebrew borrowing "quite indecisive", counted descent from a common source as one of three possibilities, and said such a source may well have come from Babylonia, where Genesis itself puts the first people after the Flood and the home of Abraham (Genesis 11:1–9; Genesis 11:31). His conclusion was that "we still do not know" how the accounts are related.
  • Both remember a real event, and Genesis keeps it truly. Alan Millard (1967) argued that borrowing has never been shown, that the differences would require a rewriting found nowhere else, and that the two accounts "undoubtedly describe the same Flood". If the Flood happened, the memory of it survived among many peoples; the Babylonians could only tell it in the language of their gods, while the Hebrews, or their ancestors, understood God's action in it. Long before, Josephus had cited Berossus and other writers of the nations as witnesses that agreed with Moses (Jewish Antiquities 1.93–95).
  • Genesis was written to answer and correct the nations' stories. Gerhard Hasel (1974) argued that Genesis 1 does not depend on the Babylonian accounts but polemicizes against them on purpose: where Atrahasis makes humans to relieve the gods of work, Genesis makes humans the "pinnacle of creation". Hasel made the argument for Genesis 1; whether the blessing of Genesis 9:1 also answers the curb on births at the end of Atrahasis is a question the texts leave open.
  • The story began in the west. Albert Clay (1922) argued, against the tide of his day, that the Flood story was Amorite or Hebrew in origin and that Babylon received it, not Israel. The sources opened for this page name no later scholar who holds this view (see "A minority view" above).

These answers can be combined: a Christian may hold that the Flood was real, that both peoples remembered it, and that Genesis was also written knowing what the nations said, to tell Israel the truth about it. The site does not decide among the Christian answers, and it does not hide the critical ones.

christian_view.h: The gods of the poem: nothing, demons, or fallen powers?
christian_view.b:
The Bible speaks of the nations' gods in more than one way, and Christians have read pagan stories in the light of each.

  • Nothing: idols are "something human hands have made" (Psalm 115:4), and "Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god" (Psalm 96:5). On this reading Anu, Enlil and Enki are inventions, and the poem is human imagination about real questions.
  • Demons: "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17), and Paul says "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20). Justin Martyr wrote that people, not knowing that these were demons, called them gods (First Apology 5). On this reading the worship the poem describes went, behind the names, to evil spirits.
  • Fallen members of God's council: Michael Heiser reads Deuteronomy 32:8, where the Most High set the nations' borders "to match the number of the sons of God", with Psalm 82, where God judges the "gods" who will "die as humans die", and argues that these are real divine beings to whom the nations were assigned, who ruled them badly. The wording of Deuteronomy 32:8 is itself disputed: the traditional Hebrew text reads "the sons of Israel"; Heiser, like the site's Plain, follows the Dead Sea Scroll reading "sons of God", which the Greek reflects as "angels of God" (see the variant at Deuteronomy 32:8). On this reading the gods of Babylon were real but rebellious powers, and the poem is their worshipers' account of them.

These are Christian readings, not the site's settled teaching. See the topic pages on the divine council, fallen angels and idolatry, and Galatians 4:8, where Paul calls them "beings who are not gods by their nature".

christian_view.h: Why the differences matter for the gospel
christian_view.b: Atrahasis gives a hard answer to the question "why are we here?": to carry the gods' basket, so they can rest. Genesis gives the opposite: God worked, finished, and rested, and blessed the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3); he made humankind in his image to rule and tend his world (Genesis 1:26–28), and he needs nothing from us (Acts 17:25). The gospel goes further still. Jesus calls the worn out and loaded down to himself to give them rest (Matthew 11:28). In the poem a god is slain so that his blood can make slaves; in the New Testament, God acquires the church "through his own blood" (Acts 20:28) to make children and heirs, not servants of a basket. (The verse has two well-known questions: the editions divide between "the church of God" and "the church of the Lord", and "his own blood" can also be read "the blood of his own one", that is, his Son; see the notes on Acts 20:28.) That is a Christian reflection on the contrast, not a claim that the poem foresaw the gospel. And after the Flood, Babylon's gods limit human life to keep the noise down, while God blesses, promises, and swears never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:1, 11; Isaiah 54:9).

cited_in.b: The Flood: a warning to one man, a boat sealed with pitch, family and animals brought aboard, a storm counted in sevens, the destruction of humankind, and a sacrifice afterward. This is the strongest link. That the accounts are related Heidel called "too obvious to require proof"; scholars disagree over how (see "Did Genesis borrow it?").

Why humankind was made. Atrahasis makes people to carry the gods' work basket; Genesis makes them in God's image, blessed to rule and fill the earth. Hasel reads Genesis 1 as a deliberate answer; Millard thought that work as the reason for humankind could have arisen in two places independently. The link is in the theme, not the wording.

Humankind made from clay, with something from the divine side: in Atrahasis the flesh and blood of a slain god, in Genesis the breath of God, two very different things. Millard notes that clay-and-spirit pictures of human making are found in many cultures, so the likeness need not mean borrowing.
Rest. In Atrahasis the gods rest once humans take their work; in Genesis God rests after finishing his own work. Millard: the actions are very similar, the contexts quite different.
Humankind multiplies on the earth before the Flood. In Atrahasis the growth itself, and its noise, is the problem; in Genesis it is the setting for the spread of evil (Genesis 6:5).

Millard noted the suggestion that the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 match the poem's spans of 1,200 years between the disasters, since both may come from counting in sixties; B. S. Childs read Genesis 6:3 instead as a limit on human life, not a period of grace, and Millard reports K. A. Kitchen on the other side. The link is weak.
The boat is sealed with pitch (Akkadian kupru, Hebrew kopher, the same word). Heidel argued that a shared technical word for bitumen does not prove borrowing.

Animals brought aboard. The Sippar copy has the hero load birds, herds and wild animals (10:61–64). The Ark Tablet, a tablet of unknown origin that SEAL files with the Middle Babylonian copies, has the hero say that wild animals went into the boat "two by two" (the verb in that line is restored), as Genesis has "two of each kind" (Genesis 6:19). A close likeness, in a broken text.
The door is shut. In Atrahasis the hero seals his own door with pitch as the storm god roars (10:76–79); in Genesis "the LORD shut the door behind him".
Sevens: Atrahasis's storm lasts "seven days and seven nights"; in Genesis God gives seven days' warning before forty days and nights of rain (Genesis 7:4, 10, 12).

The sacrifice after the Flood. The starving gods gather over Atrahasis's offering; the line is broken, and SEAL restores "smelled" and "like flies" in it, the words the Epic of Gilgamesh uses for the same scene ("The gods gathered like flies over the sacrificer", in Heidel's translation). In Genesis "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" but is not hungry, and promises not to strike every living thing again. A strong parallel, in a partly restored line.

After the Flood the gods of Atrahasis curb human numbers (barren women, infant death, priestesses who must not bear); God says "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth." The contrast is plain; whether Genesis means it as a reply cannot be shown from the texts. Hasel argued for deliberate contrast in Genesis 1, not here.
A sign hung up to remember by: the goddess's lapis lazuli "flies" (12:19–29) and God's bow in the clouds. Possible, but the lines are broken; offered on this page as Claude's theory.
Enlil cannot sleep for the noise of humankind; the LORD "does not doze and does not sleep." A contrast of pictures, not a literary link.
Noah, warned about things not yet seen, built an ark to save his household. The same event as the poem's warning of Atrahasis, read in the New Testament as an act of faith.
God guarded Noah, "a herald of righteousness", when he brought a flood on the ungodly. Compare Atrahasis summoning the elders (10:32–43), though his speech is an excuse, not a warning.

"people went on eating and drinking ... until the very day Noah went into the ark" (Matthew 24:38). Atrahasis too has a feast as the boat is loaded, with eating and drinking while the hero cannot sit for grief (10:67–74).

matches.name: Atrahasis (also Ziusudra of the Sumerian Flood Story, Utnapishtim of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Xisuthros of Berossus)
matches.b:
For: he plays the same part in the same event: warned of a flood decreed from heaven, told to build a boat and seal it, he brings his family and animals aboard, survives the storm and offers a sacrifice that the gods gather over. The Mesopotamian names belong to one figure: Millard and Heidel both identify Atrahasis with Utnapishtim of the Epic of Gilgamesh, who is also called "Atrahasis" there, and Berossus's Xisuthros goes back to Ziusudra (Heidel). Noah is the tenth generation from Adam (Genesis 5), and Berossus makes his flood hero the tenth king before the Flood (Heidel). Millard argued that Atrahasis's name may mean "exceedingly devout" and that he too is saved for his piety, as Noah was for his righteousness, and concluded that the two accounts "undoubtedly describe the same Flood".

Against: the names do not match (Noah means "rest"; Atrahasis "exceedingly wise"; Ziusudra, in Heidel's rendering, something like "he who laid hold on life of distant days"). The fathers differ: Utnapishtim is the son of Ubara-Tutu (the Opartes of Berossus), Noah the son of Lamech (Heidel). The "tenth king" comes from Berossus, writing in the 200s BC, not from the Old Babylonian poem. Atrahasis is a man of rank who summons elders, Noah a family man; Atrahasis is saved because his god breaks ranks, Noah because he found favor with the one God.

Verdict: very likely the same remembered person, for a reader who takes the Flood as a real event, as this site does. This is the site's own verdict from its Christian standpoint, not something the texts can prove.
matches.refs: Genesis 5:28–32; Genesis 6:8–9; Genesis 6:13–22; Genesis 8:20–21; Hebrews 11:7; 2 Peter 2:5

matches.name: Enki (Ea), the god who warns Atrahasis
matches.b:
For: Enki does what God does in Genesis 6:13–21: he reveals the coming flood to one man, tells him to build a boat, and so keeps life alive.

Against: Enki is one god among many, under oath with the others to destroy humankind, and he saves Atrahasis by a trick (speaking to a wall) to get around his own oath. He is the same god who planned the making of humans as laborers. In Genesis there is no second god: the God who judges is the God who warns and saves.

Verdict: unlikely. The poem divides between two gods what the Bible says one God did, and that split is the point where the two stories part.

matches.name: Enlil, the god who sends plague, drought, famine and the flood
matches.b:
For: Enlil is the ruler of the earth who decides on the Flood, as God does in Genesis 6:7, 13.

Against: Enlil acts because he cannot sleep, rages when anyone survives (12:30–35), and is rebuked by his fellow gods for acting without thought. The God of Genesis acts because of violence and evil, is grieved to his heart (Genesis 6:6), remembers Noah (Genesis 8:1) and binds himself by covenant never to do it again.

Verdict: unlikely. Heidel's judgment on Enlil's scheme was that there was little justice in it; Genesis presents the Flood as justice.

matches.name: The Igigi, the gods who rebel against their work
matches.bible: The Watchers of 1 Enoch and the sons of God of Genesis 6:2
matches.b:
For: both are divine beings who rebel in the age before the Flood, and in both the rebellion leads, by steps, to the Flood.

Against: the Igigi rebel against forced labor; nothing in the poem resembles the Watchers' crime of taking human wives and fathering giants (1 Enoch 6–7; Genesis 6:2, 4). Their strike ends not in their own fall but in the death of one god and the making of humankind to carry their work (3:33–58); whether that god was put to death as the ringleader is debated (see the notes on 2:99 and 3:48). After the Flood Enlil is "full of fury at the Igigi" (12:31), but because a man escaped, not because of the strike.

Verdict: unlikely as the same beings or the same story. The Bible does know rebellion among heavenly beings (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4), but not a strike over labor. The deeper link, that pagan gods may be real rebel powers, is a spiritual reading discussed under "The gods of the poem" above.

matches.name: The gods of the poem as a group (Anunnaki and Igigi)
matches.bible: The "sons of God" of God's heavenly council (Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 82)
matches.b:
For: on the divine-council reading argued by Michael Heiser, the nations were placed under lesser divine beings who ruled them unjustly and will "die as humans die" (Psalm 82:7); Deuteronomy 32:17 says the nations sacrificed to demons. If so, the gods Babylon worshiped were real spirits, and the poem is their worshipers' account of them, flattering and distorted.

Against: the Bible also calls these gods nothing at all (Psalm 96:5; 1 Corinthians 8:4), and the "gods" of Psalm 82 have long been read as human rulers and judges, a reading Heiser himself lists among the three main ones (see the note on Psalm 82:1 for who holds each). Deuteronomy 32:8 is a disputed text: the traditional Hebrew reads "the sons of Israel" where the Plain follows a Dead Sea Scroll's "sons of God". Nothing in the poem can identify a particular Babylonian god with a particular being in the Bible.

Verdict: possible, and only as a Christian spiritual reading, never as a fact the text can show.

matches.name: We, the slain god whose flesh and blood make humankind
matches.bible: Adam; the Bible's teaching that life is in the blood
matches.b:
For: the poem makes human life come from a god's blood and gives humans a ghost from his flesh (3:48–58), and the Bible says "a body's life is in its blood" (Leviticus 17:11) and forbids shedding human blood because humans bear God's image (Genesis 9:6). A Christian reader may also think of the death of Christ.

Against: We is a god killed so that his substance can be used; Adam is a man formed from dust who receives God's breath (Genesis 2:7). The Bible never makes humans out of a divine being's body. And Christ's death in the New Testament does not make slaves but redeems people (Acts 20:28, a verse whose wording is debated; see the notes there): the likeness is a contrast, not a memory.

Verdict: unlikely. Blood as the seat of life is an idea many peoples shared; the poem and the Bible use it in opposite ways.

matches.name: Mami (Nintu, Belet-ili), the birth goddess who makes humankind
matches.b:
For: Mami is called the maker of humankind (3:17) and mourns over people as her own children in the Flood (chapter 11); Eve is named because "she was the mother of everyone living" (Genesis 3:20).

Against: Mami is a goddess and a midwife of the gods who shapes people from clay; Eve is a created woman, the first mother by birth. The Bible's maker of humankind is God (Genesis 1:27; Isaiah 64:8), not a mother goddess.

Verdict: unlikely. If there is any link, it is that both stories have a "mother of all", but the poem gives the title to a goddess and the Bible to a woman.

matches.name: Namtar, the plague god sent by Enlil
matches.bible: The destroyer of Exodus 12:23 and the destroying angel of 2 Samuel 24:16
matches.b:
For: in both, a plague is pictured as a being sent from above, who can be stopped: Namtar lifts his hand when the people bring him offerings (chapter 5); the LORD tells the destroying angel "Enough! Now let your hand drop" (2 Samuel 24:16), and does not let the destroyer into the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:23).

Against: Namtar is Enlil's own agent ("Let Namtar quickly cut off their noise", 5:13). He is won over when the people stop worshiping their other gods and bring offerings to him alone, which put him in their debt (the Akkadian word means "be ashamed"), and so he lifts his hand. Millard, too, says the plague-god was "persuaded". By contrast, the Bible's destroyer acts only under the LORD's command and stops at his word or at the sign of the blood. The Bible never presents its destroyer as a god to be worshiped.

Verdict: unlikely as the same being; both stories share the ancient picture of plague as a messenger of death.

matches.name: The Anunnaki
matches.b:
For: both are powerful beings of the age before the Flood, and the Anunnaki rule from heaven while the Nephilim are "heroes of ancient times" on earth (Genesis 6:4), so a reader may wonder whether one story remembers the other.

Against: in the poem the Anunnaki are the great gods who rule from above (1:5) and decide the Flood together (12:32); they never come down to marry or father children. The Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 are on the earth. Nothing in the Akkadian text links the two.

Verdict: unlikely. The poem gives no ground for linking them.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what the people of Babylonia believed about their gods, about why humans exist and about the Flood, Atrahasis is excellent: it is their own sacred poem, in their own language, in a copy dated to the 1600s BC. As a text it is badly broken but well attested, in copies and fragments from the 1600s BC down to the Assyrian library at Nineveh almost a thousand years later, and later still. As history it is a story told in the language of many gods, yet it agrees with Genesis that a great Flood ended an age and one family survived it; a Christian who believes Genesis can read it as a distorted memory of that event. As theology, measured by the Bible, it gets the outline right and the meaning wrong: its gods need us, fear the Flood and starve without our offerings, while the God of the Bible needs nothing, judges evil, saves by grace and blesses life.

sections.h: 1. A witness to what its first hearers believed: very high, for the scribes and temples
sections.b: We do not have to guess what Old Babylonian scribes believed about their gods: this is their own poem, written by their own hand, dated by their king's years. It shows the ranks of the gods, the place of offerings, the fear of plague and famine, the customs of birth and marriage, and the questions they asked about work, death and the limits of life. Few ancient texts let us hear a religion so directly. This is the witness of the scribes who copied it and the temples they served; what ordinary farmers and families believed it shows less directly.

sections.h: 2. Textual reliability: good where it survives, but broken
sections.b: The text survives in many pieces of clay from Sippar, Larsa, Babylon, Nippur, Ugarit, Hattusa and Nineveh, from the 1600s BC down to late Babylonian times. That is strong evidence for the poem's wording in each period, and SEAL's score edition lets every copy be compared line by line. But no copy is complete, and Tablets II and III rest largely on one Old Babylonian copy each (B and C), with broken later pieces beside them: large parts of Tablets II and III are lost, the ending is broken, and the later copies often differ from the Old Babylonian one in wording and order. Where the Plain rests on one copy or on a restoration, the variants say so.

sections.h: 3. As history: a distorted memory of a real event?
sections.b: The poem is not history writing: its actors are gods, and its spans of 1,200 years and more are not records. A Christian who takes Genesis as true reads the poem as one people's memory of the Flood that Genesis records, kept in its outline (a warning, a boat, a family, animals, a sacrifice) but told through the lens of their gods. Millard argued that, measured by what is likely, Genesis is the more credible account. The poem cannot prove the Flood, and the Flood is not believed because of the poem; but its likeness to Genesis fits the view that many peoples remembered one great judgment. On the evidence of the ground (the flood layers at Ur and other cities, and the debate over a global or local flood), see the Genesis 7 page.

sections.h: 4. As theology, measured by the Bible
sections.b:
• Agrees: humans are made from the earth, and both stories add something from the divine side, though the two things are very different (Genesis 2:7); they are made to work (Genesis 2:15); marriage and childbirth are part of the created order (Genesis 1:27–28); a flood once destroyed humankind and one man was warned and saved (Genesis 6–8); heaven noticed the sacrifice after the Flood (Genesis 8:21).
  • Goes beyond: it tells of a time before humans when gods worked, of a strike of the lesser gods, and of a slain god. The Bible knows rebellion among heavenly beings (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4), but not gods who labor, strike over their work, or die to make humankind.
  • Conflicts: many gods rather than one (Deuteronomy 6:4); gods who tire, need food and cannot sleep (Psalm 121:4; Acts 17:25); humans made as slaves rather than as God's image (Genesis 1:26–28); a flood sent for noise rather than violence (Genesis 6:11); a hero saved by a god's trick rather than by favor (Genesis 6:8); and an order after the Flood that limits life rather than blesses it (Genesis 9:1, 8–17). On each of these the site takes the Bible's side, while describing the poem's own view fairly.

how_to_read.b: This is not Scripture, and no church has ever thought it was. It is a sacred poem of Babylon's gods, translated so that you can see the world Abraham came from and the stories Israel's neighbors told. Read it with respect for the people who wrote it: they were asking real questions. Read it critically too, as a Christian reader would, testing it by what God has said.

Read 1:1–3:107 with Genesis 1–2; 5:1–9:176 with Genesis 6:1–8; and 10:1–12:115 with Genesis 6:9–9:17. Ask at each step: what is the same, what is different, and what does the difference say about God? The notes and the side-by-side section above will help.

how_to_read.h: Do not build on the broken places
how_to_read.b: Many of the most striking lines are partly restored or broken. A theory that rests on a lost word is weak, however exciting it sounds. Where the notes say "the line is broken", believe them.

The quickest way into the poem is to notice what its gods need: rest, sleep, quiet, food and drink. Then read Psalm 121:4 and Acts 17:24–25, and notice that the God of the Bible needs none of these, and gives them instead (Matthew 11:28).
